content: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most common life-threatening genetic disorder in white populations. It leads to various complications, including postural abnormalities. These abnormalities can result in pain, deformities of the trunk, and a reduced quality of life. Physical therapy has been proposed as a potential intervention to address these issues. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of different physical therapy techniques on postural abnormalities in individuals with CF, specifically focusing on their impact on quality of life, pain, and trunk deformities. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. The search also included hand-searched journals, conference abstracts, and reference lists of relevant articles. The last search was performed on March 19, 2020. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared any form of physical therapy relevant to postural abnormalities against other physical therapies, no therapy, sham treatments, or standard medical care. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of the trials, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data. Missing or additional information was sought from the trial authors. The quality of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE criteria. Two trials, involving a total of 50 participants with CF and postural abnormalities, met the inclusion criteria. One trial included individuals with stable CF over a three-month period, while the other involved hospitalized patients experiencing an exacerbation over 20 days. Both trials were conducted in the UK and compared manual therapy interventions to standard medical care. The manual therapy interventions included rib cage and thoracic spine mobilizations, treatment of specific muscle dysfunctions or tight muscle groups, and postural education and awareness. Participants ranged in age from 17 to 58 years. The outcomes measured in these trials included changes in quality of life, pain, trunk deformity, and pulmonary function. The evidence suggested that manual therapy may have little to no effect on trunk deformity when compared to usual care, but this conclusion was based on low-quality evidence. Due to significant variability between the trials, no meaningful analysis could be performed for quality of life or pain outcomes, and the evidence for these outcomes was rated as very low quality. Similarly, it remains uncertain whether manual therapy improves lung function, as the evidence for forced vital capacity (FVC), forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), and Tiffeneau’s index (FEV1/FVC ratio) was also of very low quality. One of the trials, which included 15 participants, assessed functional capacity by measuring the distance walked. The results suggested a potential benefit of the intervention over usual care, but the wide confidence intervals indicated the possibility of no effect. This trial also reported that six participants in the intervention group provided positive feedback about the therapy, and no adverse events were noted. In conclusion, the evidence regarding the benefits of physical therapies for postural abnormalities in individuals with CF is limited due to the methodological weaknesses of the included trials and the very low to low quality of the available evidence. Further research is needed, with well-designed trials that include clear criteria for identifying participants with postural abnormalities.
